stages.title: Advanced linguistics and grammar
stages.hook: The verb qāla ("he said") becomes qultu ("I said"), not qalatu. What happened to the middle letter?
explain: Arabic grammar was first described systematically by scholars of Basra and Kufa. Sibawayh (8th century) wrote al-Kitāb, the foundation of the grammatical tradition. Terms that survive today: fāʿil (subject), mafʿūl bihi (direct object), mubtadaʾ and khabar (subject and predicate of a nominal sentence), and iʿrāb (case and mood endings: marfūʿ, manṣūb, majrūr).

Roots are strong or weak. A weak root contains w, y or hamza. Hollow verbs have a weak middle letter: q-w-l gives qāla (he said) but qultu (I said), because the long vowel shortens before a consonant ending. Defective verbs have a weak last letter, such as ramā (he threw) and ramaytu (I threw).

Some nouns are diptotes (mamnūʿ min aṣ-ṣarf), which take no tanwīn and use -a instead of -i in the genitive: li-Aḥmada. Such details show that Arabic grammar is a system of patterns, with predictable exceptions.
stages.mnemonic: Weak letters are shy: they shrink or change when something is added after them.
sentences: Sibawayh wrote an important book on grammar.
The subject is nominative and the object is accusative.
Weak verbs change when they are conjugated.

gq.q: Why is the past of q-w-l "qultu" (I said) and not "qawaltu"?
o: The weak middle letter becomes a short vowel before the consonant ending
The root is irregular and cannot be explained
gq.why: In hollow verbs the long vowel shortens before a consonant suffix.

gq.q: What is a diptote (mamnūʿ min aṣ-ṣarf)?
o: A noun with no tanwīn and a genitive in -a
A noun that is always definite
gq.why: Diptotes such as Aḥmad take -a in the genitive and no tanwīn.

panel.q: What does the grammatical term iʿrāb refer to?
o: The case and mood endings that show a word's function
panel.why: Iʿrāb is the system of final vowel endings.

panel.q: In ramaytu (I threw) from ramā, what is the weak letter, and what kind of verb is it?
o: The last letter y; a defective verb
The first letter; an assimilated verb
The middle letter; a hollow verb
panel.why: The root r-m-y ends in a weak letter, so the verb is defective.

panel.q: Why is knowing the root-and-pattern system useful for understanding irregular-looking verbs?
panel.model: Apparent irregularities follow rules for weak roots: once you identify the root and pattern, the changes (such as shortening of long vowels) are predictable.
panel.why: Irregularities are systematic.

teach.model: Arabic grammar was described by early scholars like Sibawayh. Words have roots and patterns. Weak roots with w, y or hamza change in predictable ways. Case endings show the function of a word.

points.ask: What are roots and weak verbs?

stages.title: Historical development of the language
stages.hook: The English words "algebra", "coffee", "sugar" and "zero" all came through Arabic. What does that tell you about the history of the language?
explain: Arabic belongs to the Semitic family with Hebrew, Aramaic, Amharic and others. Its earliest long texts are pre-Islamic poems such as the Muʿallaqāt, composed in a high poetic language. The Qurʾān (7th century) became a lasting model for Classical Arabic (al-fuṣḥā), and grammarians then recorded its rules.

Under the Abbasids in Baghdad, a great translation movement brought Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic, creating scientific vocabulary. Words such as al-jabr (algebra), ṣifr (zero), qahwa (coffee) and sukkar (sugar) later entered European languages. The Nahda (19th-century revival) modernised Arabic for press, schools and science, and language academies coined terms.

Over centuries the spoken varieties diverged into dialects, while MSA became the shared written standard. Historical linguists reconstruct this development from inscriptions, manuscripts and comparing dialects, and scholars still debate how early the dialects separated.
stages.mnemonic: Baghdad's House of Wisdom: a bridge that carried knowledge both ways.
sentences: Arabic belongs to the Semitic language family.
Many scientific books were translated into Arabic in Baghdad.
The word algebra comes from Arabic.

gq.q: Which language belongs to the same family as Arabic?
gq.why: Hebrew and Arabic are both Semitic. Persian and Turkish belong to other families.
The Nahda modernised Arabic culture and language.

panel.q: Why do historians say Arabic transmitted knowledge to Europe?
o: Works were translated into Arabic, developed, and later translated into Latin
panel.why: The translation chain helped carry mathematical and medical knowledge.

panel.q: Why do linguists disagree about when the dialects split from Classical Arabic?
o: Early spoken language was not recorded and evidence is indirect
panel.why: The debate rests on limited early evidence.

panel.q: Explain the roles of the Qurʾān and the Abbasid translation movement in the history of Arabic.
panel.model: The Qurʾān gave a lasting model for Classical Arabic; the translation movement under the Abbasids created scientific vocabulary by moving Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic.
panel.why: Both shaped the standard language and its vocabulary.

teach.model: Arabic is a Semitic language. Pre-Islamic poetry and the Qurʾān shaped the classical standard. The Abbasid translation movement added scientific terms, and the Nahda modernised Arabic.

stages.title: Literature and cultural discourse
stages.hook: A medieval author told stories in rhymed prose where the same hero appears in a new city each time. What is this form?
explain: Arabic literary history has long strands. The Muʿallaqāt are pre-Islamic odes. In the Abbasid period, al-Jāḥiẓ wrote lively prose, and the maqāma (e.g. by al-Hamadhānī and al-Ḥarīrī) tells short tales in rhymed prose (sajʿ), often about a clever trickster. Ibn Khaldūn's Muqaddima (14th century) analyses history and society.

In the modern period, writers like Nāzik al-Malāʾika and Badr Shākir as-Sayyāb in Iraq pioneered free verse (shiʿr ḥurr) in the late 1940s. The Arab novel developed in the 20th century, and Naguib Mahfouz won the Nobel Prize in 1988. Debates about turāth (heritage) and ḥadātha (modernity) shape cultural discourse.
To discuss a text, place it in its genre, period and audience, then read closely. Avoid broad claims about "the Arab mind"; discuss specific works, authors and contexts.
stages.mnemonic: Maqāma: a story in a "standing place" of words where rhyme is the stage.
sentences: Ibn Khaldun wrote the Muqaddima about history and society.
The maqama is a tale in rhymed prose.

gq.why: Sajʿ is prose with rhyming phrase endings.

gq.q: Which two poets are linked with free verse in Iraq?
o: Nāzik al-Malāʾika and Badr Shākir as-Sayyāb
gq.why: They pioneered shiʿr ḥurr in the 1940s.

panel.q: Why is the Muqaddima studied outside literature classes too?
o: It analyses history and society and influenced later thinkers
panel.why: Ibn Khaldūn's work is important in historiography and social thought.

panel.q: Why is the phrase "the Arab mind" a poor basis for literary analysis?
o: It makes sweeping claims about millions of different people instead of discussing specific texts
panel.why: Good analysis is specific.

panel.q: Explain the debate between turāth (heritage) and ḥadātha (modernity) in Arab culture.
panel.model: Writers and thinkers debate how to relate to inherited traditions and classical culture while taking part in modern ideas and forms, such as free verse and the novel; some seek balance, others stress one side.
panel.why: The debate is about continuity and change.

teach.model: Arabic literature includes pre-Islamic odes, maqāma stories in rhymed prose, Ibn Khaldūn's Muqaddima, free verse and modern novels. Discuss specific works and contexts.

points.ask: What is new in modern poetry?

stages.title: Advanced academic writing
stages.hook: How does an academic writer show that an idea came from someone else, and why does it matter?
explain: University writing in Arabic is formal MSA. It uses the abstract (mulakhkhaṣ), introduction, literature review (murājaʿat al-adabiyyāt), method, results, discussion and conclusion. Sources are acknowledged in footnotes (hawāmish) and a list of references (qāʾimat al-marājiʿ). A direct quotation (iqtibās) is put in quotation marks or marked with « ».

Plagiarism (intiḥāl or saraqa ʿilmiyya) is using someone's words or ideas without credit. Paraphrasing still needs a citation. Hedging and careful claims are valued: tushīru n-natāʾij ilā anna ... (the results point to ...).

Style tips: prefer verbal nouns and the passive for objectivity, keep sentences clear, avoid dialect and personal anecdotes, and use consistent terminology. The Arabic comma (،) and semicolon (؛) are normal; Western or Eastern digits should be used consistently.
stages.mnemonic: Idea + credit = scholarship; idea without credit = theft.
sentences: Every quotation must be linked to its source.
The study aims to examine the effect of reading.
The literature review precedes the method.

gq.q: Is a paraphrase without a citation acceptable?
o: No: ideas must be credited even when reworded
Yes: only exact words need credit
gq.why: Plagiarism includes using ideas without crediting them.

gq.q: What goes in the qāʾimat al-marājiʿ?
o: The sources used in the work

panel.q: A student translates an English article into Arabic and submits it as their own. Why is this plagiarism?
o: The ideas and structure are not theirs and no source is credited
It is only a problem if it is long
panel.why: Translation without credit still uses someone else's work.

panel.q: Why prefer "tushīru n-natāʾij ilā anna" to "I think"?
o: It places the claim on evidence and keeps an academic tone
panel.why: Impersonal hedging is the academic norm.

panel.q: Explain how to avoid plagiarism in an Arabic research paper.
panel.model: Credit every source in footnotes and a reference list, put exact words in quotation marks and paraphrase honestly with a citation.
panel.why: Honest attribution is central to scholarship.

teach.model: A university paper has an abstract, literature review, method, results and conclusion. Cite every source in footnotes and a reference list. Plagiarism means using ideas or words without credit.

points.ask: What sections does a paper have?

stages.title: Professional translation
stages.hook: A contract translated for a court must be exact. What extra steps might a professional translator take?
explain: Professional translation covers legal, medical, technical and commercial texts. A certified translation (tarjama muʿtamada) carries the translator's declaration and sometimes a stamp, so authorities accept it. Translators build a glossary (masrad muṣṭalaḥāt) for consistent terminology and follow a style guide (dalīl uslūb).

Quality control includes revision by a second person (murājaʿa) and proofreading (tadqīq lughawī). Localisation (tawṭīn) adapts a text to the target audience: dates, units, names, politeness and design. Arabic texts run right to left, but numbers and Latin words inside them run left to right, so formatting checks are essential.

Common problems: dialect words in formal texts, terms that vary by country (for example "computer": ḥāsūb or kumbyūtar), and Hijri versus Gregorian dates. When uncertain, the translator asks the client, adds a note, and does not guess.
stages.mnemonic: Glossary first, translate second, review third.
sentences: The translator prepares a glossary before starting.
Another person must review the translation.
Numbers and dates need careful attention.

o: To use the same term for the same concept throughout
gq.why: Consistency in terminology is a key quality factor.

o: Adapting dates, units and style to the target audience
gq.why: It makes a text suitable for the local readers.

panel.q: A translated Arabic report shows "12/05/2024". Why must the translator check this?
o: Day-month order and calendar (Hijri or Gregorian) may differ
panel.why: Date formats vary and could cause serious errors.

panel.q: Why is a second reviewer valuable?
o: A fresh reader catches errors and awkward wording
It is mandatory in all countries
panel.why: Revision improves quality.

panel.q: A term has two Arabic equivalents used in different countries. What should a professional translator do?
panel.model: Find out the target audience or ask the client, choose one equivalent, record it in the glossary and use it consistently.
panel.why: Professionals decide and document terminology.

teach.model: Professional translators work with legal, medical and technical texts. They build a glossary, keep terms consistent and have the work reviewed. Certified translation is accepted by authorities.

points.ask: How do I keep terms consistent?

stages.title: Interpretation of complex communication
stages.hook: Someone says "We will see, God willing." Is it a promise, a polite no, or something else? How could you tell?
explain: Interpreting complex communication means understanding more than words. Pragmatics studies how context shapes meaning. A phrase like in shāʾ Allāh can mean a sincere plan, a hopeful wish or a polite way to avoid commitment; tone, situation and what follows decide.

Speakers may be indirect to be polite (mujāmala): a refusal can be softened with "ṣaʿb qalīlan" (a little difficult) or an offer of an alternative. Compliments, invitations and offers may follow repeated rituals. A literal (ḥarfī) reading can miss the intended meaning (qaṣd); a figurative (majāzī) reading can be too much. Always avoid stereotyping: practices differ by country, class, age and person.
Ask clarifying questions when stakes are high, note speaker tone and body language, and give the listener the meaning and the function, not only the words.
stages.mnemonic: Words are the box; intention is the gift inside.
sentences: The speaker's intention is not always clear from the words.
Tone changes the meaning of the sentence.

gq.why: Pragmatics is about meaning in use.
Qaṣd is the speaker's intended meaning.

panel.q: An interpreter renders every "in shāʾ Allāh" as "I promise". What is the risk?
o: The speaker may mean only a wish or a polite non-commitment
Nothing, it is always a promise
panel.why: Different functions need different renderings.

panel.q: Why should a listener avoid generalising, such as "Arabs never say no directly"?
o: Communication styles vary by person, place and context
panel.why: Generalisations are inaccurate and stereotyping.

panel.q: How can an interpreter handle an unclear indirect refusal?
panel.model: Notice the tone and context, ask a clarifying question if possible, and convey the intended function rather than only the literal words.
panel.why: Meaning depends on context and intention.

teach.model: Meaning depends on context, tone and intention. Phrases like in shāʾ Allāh can mean different things. Interpreters check context and clarify when needed, and avoid stereotypes.

points.ask: What should an interpreter do if unclear?

stages.title: Language variation and dialectology
stages.hook: The letter qāf is a deep "q" in MSA, but Cairenes often say a glottal stop and many Gulf speakers say "g". What does one letter reveal about variation?
explain: Dialectology studies how varieties differ and why. One famous variable is ق (qāf): [q] in MSA and many rural/Bedouin speech varieties, [ʔ] (glottal stop) in Cairo and Damascus city speech, [g] in Gulf, Upper Egypt and many Bedouin dialects. The letter ج (jīm) is [dʒ] in MSA, [ʒ] in the Levant and Maghreb and [g] in Cairo.

Grammar also varies: negation (Egyptian mā ... sh), future markers (Egyptian ḥa-, Levantine raḥ-, Moroccan ghādī), and the progressive prefix b- in Egyptian and Levantine. Speakers also borrow: Maghrebi Arabic has French and Amazigh words, Gulf Arabic has Persian, Hindi and English words.

Sociolinguists study urban (ḥaḍar), rural and Bedouin (badw) varieties, and code-switching between MSA and dialect. Dialects are full linguistic systems, not "broken Arabic"; labels like "better" and "worse" are social, not linguistic, judgments.
stages.mnemonic: Same letter, many voices: qāf wears a different hat in every city.
sentences: The letter qāf is pronounced in different ways in the dialects.
Speakers change code according to the situation.
The dialects borrowed words from other languages.

gq.q: In which speech is ق typically pronounced as a glottal stop?
o: City speech of Cairo and Damascus
gq.why: Cairene and Damascene urban speech use [ʔ].

o: Moving between varieties or languages within a conversation
gq.why: Speakers shift according to topic, audience and setting.

panel.q: A learner says one dialect is "broken Arabic". What is a linguist's response?
o: Dialects are complete systems with their own rules; prestige is social
panel.why: Linguistics treats varieties as equally systematic.

panel.q: Which feature marks the future in Levantine speech?
panel.why: Raḥ is Levantine; ḥa- is Egyptian; ghādī is Moroccan; sawfa is MSA.

panel.q: Why is the qāf a good example for studying dialect variation?
panel.model: Because the same letter has several regular pronunciations across regions and social groups, so speakers can be identified and sound change can be studied.
panel.why: Qāf is a classic sociolinguistic variable.

teach.model: Dialectology compares varieties. The letter qāf is pronounced as q, a glottal stop or g in different places. Grammar and loanwords also vary. Dialects are full systems.

points.ask: What is an example of variation?
Why do dialects have different words?

stages.title: Specialised scientific or technical language
stages.hook: The word "algorithm" comes from the name of a Baghdad scholar. How do languages create new scientific words?
explain: Arabic creates technical terms by derivation, calque and borrowing. Derivation uses roots and patterns: ḥāsūb (computer) from ḥ-s-b, "to calculate"; mukhtabar (laboratory) from kh-b-r, "to know by experience". Calques translate parts: shabaka (network). Loanwords include kumbyūtar and biyūlūjī, and academies recommend native alternatives, so several terms may coexist.

Scientific vocabulary: khuwārizmiyya (algorithm, after al-Khwārizmī), muʿādala (equation), khaliyya (cell), ṭāqa (energy), tajriba (experiment), bayānāt (data), barmajiyyāt (software). Some terms differ by country, so check the audience and reference works.

Technical writing is precise and impersonal: it uses definitions, the passive, numbered steps and units. The Arabic digits may be Eastern (٣) or Western (3), and decimal separators may differ (٫ or ,), so state conventions clearly.
stages.mnemonic: Root + pattern = new term: ḥ-s-b gives ḥāsūb, the "calculator".
sentences: The scientist conducted an experiment in the laboratory.
The algorithm processes the data quickly.
Solar energy is a renewable source.

gq.q: From which scholar's name does the Arabic word khuwārizmiyya (algorithm) come?
gq.why: The word derives from the name of al-Khwārizmī, the Baghdad mathematician.

gq.q: What is a calque in technical terms?
o: A term built by translating the parts of a foreign term

panel.q: Why can "computer" appear as ḥāsūb in one text and kumbyūtar in another?
o: Different countries and institutions prefer a native or a borrowed term
panel.why: Usage varies; check the audience.

panel.q: Why should a technical translator state number conventions (٣ or 3, decimal mark)?
o: Readers may misread values if the convention is unclear
All readers use the same convention
panel.why: Clarity avoids costly errors.

panel.q: Describe two ways Arabic forms new scientific terms.
panel.model: It derives words from roots and patterns (ḥāsūb from ḥ-s-b) and it borrows or translates foreign terms (calques such as shabaka), with academies suggesting standards.
panel.why: Terminology uses derivation and borrowing.

teach.model: Arabic forms scientific terms from roots and patterns, by translating foreign terms and by borrowing. Terms can differ by country, so check your audience. Technical writing is precise and impersonal.

points.ask: Are the terms the same everywhere?

stages.title: Integrated proficiency project
stages.hook: Imagine you must read an Arabic article, summarise it, answer it in writing and present your view. Which skills from this course would you combine?
explain: The final project combines reading, writing, speaking and interpretation at an advanced level (about CEFR C1). A model task: read an MSA article on a social or scientific issue; summarise it (talkhīṣ) in your own words; write a response with a thesis, evidence and a recommendation (tawṣiya); then present orally with a clear structure and answer questions.

Use the tools you have learned: root-and-pattern guessing for new words, connectors for coherence, iʿrāb for accurate endings, register control for MSA versus dialect, and culture-aware pragmatics. Name the dialect if you quote one and give sources for facts.
Evaluate your work with feedback (taghdhiya rājiʿa): check meaning, accuracy, range of vocabulary, fluency and register. A portfolio (milaff injāz) keeps drafts and reflections, showing progress.
stages.mnemonic: Read, sum up, respond, speak, reflect: R-S-R-S-R.
sentences: The project combines reading, writing and speaking.
I recommend using Standard Arabic in the report.
Feedback helps us improve our language.

gq.q: In a portfolio, what is the main purpose?
gq.why: A portfolio collects work to show progress.

panel.q: A summary repeats whole sentences from the article. What should the writer change?
o: Rewrite the main ideas in their own words and cite the source
panel.why: A summary condenses ideas in your own words.

panel.q: Which register best suits a written report to a university?
panel.why: Formal MSA is the norm for academic reports.

panel.q: List the steps of an integrated Arabic project from reading to presenting.
panel.model: Read the article, summarise it, write a response with evidence and a recommendation, present orally and use feedback to improve.
panel.why: The project integrates all four skills.

teach.model: Read an article, summarise it in your own words, write a response with a recommendation, present it and reflect on feedback. Use formal MSA and name any dialect you quote.
